utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Judge Fluegge draws my attention to page 45, and it just disappeared from my screen. Let's see. Line 16. Could you please give it some -- could you give it some thought on whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To explain it. Is that correct killed by the ABiH or should it be killed by the VRS? Perhaps you can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Which page I'm 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 45, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 45, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That were considered killed by the ABiH list. That are registered as killed I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Think that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Considered by the ABiH killed rather than by whom they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is a common understanding of what the witness said, I don't think there's any need to clarify with the witness. Once the witness has put her earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to look at Exhibit D344 in e-court. And if it assist you, I have a copy of that in hard copy in the Serbian language -- oh, never mind. It won't help. The Serbian doesn't have the graphs. And, first of all, did you have occasion to review this memorandum during your preparations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And taking into account the date of the same, what does this appear to relate to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with a Defence request and some data need to verified in terms of whether there were soldiers on the OTP lists or not. They explain that they ran their checks, they explain their approach, and they explain that they established that there were some 70 per cent of them, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at Table number 2 -- table -- Annex 2, which is on page 5 in English, and page 5 in the Serbian. It should be the next page in the Serbian. Page 6 in Serbian, I apologise. So that, Professor, can you see the heading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Is it correct to broadcast this list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instruction has been given not to broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, you see the title on the Serbian translation but the graph or the table is the same for both languages there is no translation of the table. Having had a chance to look at this, do you have any comments about what is the significance of the information that is provided herein?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the table only. There's something on the left-hand side, and I can't see the table properly. Could the table be enlarged, please. So, in 2008, the Demographic Unit reacted to a Defence request, confirming that there were soldiers on their list and that they matched some 70.1 per cent of overall cases. There were also 228 cases of soldiers for whom the ABiH claimed had been killed before 1995 and yet they were on the list as Srebrenica victims. In this reply, they state that they looked into those 220-plus cases and that, in the meantime, they requested clarifications from the ABiH. They also state that in some 137 cases or so, they received confirmation that the date was incorrect and that it was corrected. They also state that in a certain number of cases, the ABiH did not state whether they were killed or not. In another 38 cases, no reply was received, and they were still awaiting one. This document is characteristic in putting the sign of equation between the ABiH list and the list of the international centre of persons on the one mapped, and, on the other hand, that it only presents a table. I think it would have been intellectually honest, in terms of all the answers they received from the ABiH, which must have been received as some kind of confirmation or certificates, then those -- for those certificates attached so that we can see how corrections were made. This was also not the first set of corrections made by the ABiH. In some previous cases, I also had occasion to see that the ABiH did correct some data upon the request of OTP experts. All I can say is that I am surprised because if it occurred before, it would have been logical to ask the ABiH to revise their lists, rather than whenever you come across something, you send it back to the ABiH to have it corrected or not. The fact that they rely on the ICRC lists points to that fact. They keep saying that these are revised lists. The ICRC lists contains those who were missing and now with the addition of those for whom certain proof of death was received. Apparently they had an agreement in place with the ABiH not to revise the lists from 2001 in order for the ABiH to send a final list of sorts. Another interesting thing is that the OTP experts believe that the persons on the list of the international committee for identifying missing persons who are considered dead, the OTP investigators believed that they were positively killed in 1995. It is a well known fact that this committee, which engages in identifying exhumed mortal remains, they do so through DNA analysis. DNA analysis is not a method on the basis of which one can prove when and where somebody died. By DNA analysis, you simply ascertain that this person has this or that name. I listened to Dr. Thomas Parsons' testimony who for a while was one of the directors of that committee, and he absolutely confirmed that one cannot use DNA analysis to ascertain the place and date of death. I am not disputing that these people were exhumed, but I don't know when they were killed. The experts don't know that, who carry out autopsies. They can only say, as forensic pathologists, where those people were found, in which graves. Therefore, I don't know how the OTP experts used that to prove that these people were killed in 1995. On the basis of what? I could understand if they only concluded that they were simply dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could return to the matching keys for a second and for that, we need P1900, page 86 in Serbian and 81 in the English, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. While waiting for that. Witness, you said: "Apparently they had a agreement in place with the ABiH not to revise the lists in order for the ABiH to send a final list of sorts." What's the basis for telling us that apparently there was agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I intended to say. It may have been misinterpreted. What I said was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second before you continue. By saying perhaps you were misinterpreted, you're more or less hinting at our interpreters to be blamed for it and not for you using the language as it was translated to us. Do you want it to be verified? Because we are able to do so. Then we listen -- not we. But, again, the B/C/S will be listened at, and then we'll establish whether or not you correctly or incorrectly hinted at our interpreters who made a mistake rather than, perhaps, you yourself. Is that what you wish us to do, then we'll gladly do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I do not doubt the interpreters. I said that they could have agreed, and I'm not saying that an interpreter did that on purpose. Or the interpreter. The OTP experts received these databases from the army and the appropriate Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they could only receive them if they had inquired into their existence. Nobody sent those voluntarily. Those databases exist as of 2001 in the Demographic Unit of the OTP. I apologise. Let me complete my answer so as to avoid any confusion. If they are there and if there had been cases whereby requests were made to verify some information from the databases, if I matched the year from the database and then there's a correction made to a case, then it must mean that the army did revise or could have revised their lists. In that case, the OTP experts could have asked for the revised list, rather than go individually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's all theory. What could have happened. Whereas, you suggested in your answer -- or even by saying they could have done this, that is hinting at what they apparently failed to do and that's how I understand your observation in the context of your answer. But apparently is not what you intended to say, I do understand, so, therefore, we can proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we have the keys used by the Prosecution before us. Dr. Brunborg when he testified about the use of these keys, he said the following at transcript page 15203, line 2 through 15204, line 2: "However, we did not accept these matches without consulting and comparing other pieces of information like place of birth and date of birth was there, of course, about you place of birth and other available information to see if he -- if it was likely that these 255 matches concerned the same persons and so we did that, trying -- trying to be imaginative and tried different criteria. This is a methodology called fuzzy matching. If you don't have exact data, we need to do fuzzy matching and try out different things. In some countries, like my own Norway, we only use one criteria for matching data from various sources, and that is the personal identification number, but that number in the former Yugoslavia was not used by everybody, and there was -- there were many errors in the lists that we had available where that number was, so we had to use other -- we had to use name and other kinds of information. In modern matching techniques there are now, I've learned methods that apply probabilities to matches. We don't. When I started doing this work, I wasn't aware of this methodology, and also in -- in legal cases, you cannot really rely on probabilities because you need to be absolutely certain. I don't think the Court would have been satisfied with, say, with there's an 80 per cent probability that this person is the same in the ICRC lists and in the census, for example, so that's why we used all this different criteria. I see criterion 22 resulted in 2078 matches, whereas the two previous criterias did not result in any. And the last criteria on number 71 resulted in one person, as far as I remember, so this is a perfectly valid methodology that, as I, let me repeat, that we always compared and checked whether the matches that came up in less than ideal, with less -- with less than ideal criteria were highly likely." Now, Professor, I'd ask you to comment upon this fuzzy method of matching that Dr. Brunborg is talking about. Does it provide a probability that the person has been matched, or is it an absolute certainty that the person has been correctly matched, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this fuzzy matching method is being used, then one has to say where it's being used. Dr. Brunborg had to do that. For example, in enormous research involving millions perhaps that can be used. But you are giving information at aggregate level. When you give data, you do not give it at an individual level. If I understood that correctly Dr. Brunborg says in his country, one, just one criterion, and it's numerical. He first heard of some methods when he came here, he says due to the problems that he has with data sources concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, would you mind to answer the question, whether it's about probabilities or about certainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't know where it's used, and most probably it is probability. Probability that something matched, coincided.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In reference to these keys that we on the screen, would you describe any part of these keys as being probabilities rather than absolute certainties?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that even the first criteria that I would accept is high probability, not 100 per cent uncertainty because you have the name, father's name, surname, and place of birth, municipality of birth, and now in the English translation, there's also the municipality of death, not to give any comment on that now. Now, if you take a small number, statistically small, that is, if you run it in 4.3 million names, surnames, years, dates, with a large number of errors that are primarily reflected in the names and surnames, then if you get matches in terms of date of birth and place of birth, it is highly likely that it is the same person. For example, if it says Svetlana Radonovic, somewhere, rather than Radovanovic. Now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, how many persons are this with the same name, the same surname, the same father's name, the same date of birth, and place of birth, I don't know. I don't think that it is significant, a significant figure from a statistical point of view among 4 million people. However, I think that the first criterion is high probability. But that is also probability. It is not anything absolute, In order to be able to claim absolutely that it is a particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, you may have just done it but in lines 19 through 20 of temporary transcript page 55, the English translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The English translation of your - first paragraph - answer states as follows: "I claim that even the first criteria that I would accept is how probability, not 100 per cent uncertainty." And in relation to that first part of your answer, could you comment or correct what we have received.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is high probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is [Overlapping speakers] ... that is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, but your attention was asked for what then followed, I take it, you then recorded as having said: Not 100 per cent uncertainty. Did you say or did you intend to say not 100 per cent certainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainty. Certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you've already mentioned, I believe, that the -- lack of using mortality rates by the Prosecution experts. Dr. Tabeau, at transcript page 19401 said that she actually did make reference to mortality rates in one report as to Sarajevo. And I'd like to look at that with you and that is 65 ter number 11855, and it will be page 38 in both the Serbian and the English. And it's the report for the Galic case and it will be Table number 15. And I'd like to ask you: What is your observation of how Dr. Tabeau incorporated mortality rates, in relation to this one instance where she said that she did use mortality rates?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are mortality rates for 1991 and for 1990. They are provided for certain municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are presented in terms of populations of 100.000. Death rates in Bosnia-Herzegovina and anywhere are usually registered in terms of thousands of inhabitants. Now, what does this mean? What do these rates mean? They show the frequency of death and if we say that the rate of death is, say, ten "promil" that means that for every 1.000 inhabitants of a town or a country, et cetera, ten inhabitants die. The entire statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina including this presents general death rates in "promil," so it is 1.000 inhabitants that are taken into account. Dr. Tabeau here uses 100.000. I really don't know why. But when you do it this way, with 100.000 you can see certain absurdities. For instance, look at the municipality of Vogosca. It's the last municipality in this list. In 1991, it had 24.647 inhabitants. When will Vogosca have 100.000 inhabitants that so that 1.123 persons will die per 100.000. I doubt that that that would happen in this millennium unless gold and diamonds are found there. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Radovanovic, this is just mathematics. It doesn't say anywhere that in Vogosca you would have 100.000. It's just about percentages, isn't it? Does it make any say that there are not 100.000 people in Vogosca for this purposes? Are you serious about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not percentages. That's the problem. The death rate shows the frequency of dying and if it is expressed in terms of 100.000 inhabitants then are you showing the frequency of dying -- how many people were -- will die within 100.000 inhabitants? Vogosca doesn't that have that many inhabitants, never will have that many inhabitants. Now the entire statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina expressed it in the following way. It is the death rate in terms of 1.000 and then you can say per 1.000 inhabitants in Vogosca, 11 or 12 persons die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that you just move the comma two the left and that you have the same number? About the death rate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the death rate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You say it's the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is calculated in the following way. The number of deceased is divided by the number of inhabitants and you multiply all of that by 1.000 or 100.000. That is how this death rate is calculated. It would not be 112. It would be 11.2 had the figure of 1.000 inhabitants been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you moved the comma two to the left and then have you the same outcome? I mean, what we're talking about, that in a certain year, and let's just take 1991, 135 people died on a population of 24.000. That is simply, approximately a death rate of five, isn't it, on thousand? You divide 135 by 24 and you're at a death rate for 1.000. If you take 100.000, it's multiplied by 100. It's the same in accordance to -- to what you -- how do you find the death rate. Do you calculate it for 100.000 or do you calculate it for 1.000? And the outcome will be just hundred times bigger or smaller. Isn't that the simple mathematics which you're criticizing here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is presented in a way that would leave a stronger impression. When you're a demographer this is how you read it, that in Vogosca in 1990 and 1991, 1.123 persons died per 100.000 inhabitants and that's how each and every demographer would read this. And then that is absurd, if Vogosca doesn't have that kind of population to begin with. However from a technical point of view for you to be able to calculate it this way and that way, that's fine. Both death rates can be dealt with that way. 100.000, 1.000, I repeat. All of Bosnia-Herzegovina expressed its statistics per thousand. But if you would now just present the death rates for Vogosca you would see that 1.123 persons die per 100.000 inhabitants. That is how this death rate is read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move it left or right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. We read it as it is presented by the expert. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to your report, D1211, marked for identification and page 56 in the Serbian, page 57 in the English, and your Figure 4, which I believe you should still have the hard copy of from yesterday. And I'd ask to you explain for us what you are demonstrating in this figure in your report that we now have before us.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows the results that are obtained if you use a relatively reliable criterion for matching or if you use the methods of the OTP experts. In 2007 or 2008, I can't remember exactly, I matched the Prosecution list where the Srebrenica victims are, the people they consider to be the victims, according to the criterion name, father's name, surname, not date of birth, but year of birth, and these are the results that I obtained. So that's the criterion that says name, father's name, surname, and year of birth. These are the results obtained. So I'm just showing that the number of criteria was smaller. Or more reliable. Or perhaps what -- or, rather, had it been that way, it would have been different. Had there been fewer but more reliable criteria, then different matching results would be obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to page 58 in the English and page 57 in the Serbian and your table number 9, could you walk us through what you are demonstrating here.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this information is taken from expert reports that have to do with Srebrenica. Prosecution expert reports. And this is the way in which certain percentages and shares were supposed to be calculated as it is done in a methodologically correct way. I took the total number of male population in 1991 in the area that they considered to be Srebrenica. That is to say, these five municipalities and then I said what the Prosecution findings were and what -- oh, sorry, I profoundly apologise to the interpreters. Now, what are the findings of the OTP experts? Missing persons. Then I looked at the findings of the international centre for identification, and then I took the information from the Red Cross and I calculated the percentages in relation to all of that. And you see these percentages fall within this range. And then I looked at missing persons. And I calculated the percentages. These percentages are calculated in this way without any kind of invention. You have the dead, you have the population figures, that is the only way in which you can do this calculation. You cannot calculate this on the basis of age from 1995, because you do not have the number of inhabitants in 1995. And it makes no sense to calculate it on the basis of age from 1991 because these are apples and oranges. In addition to that, in order to get to any kind of percentage share in terms of municipalities for 1995 and in order to assess the population, the number of inhabitants in addition to the fact that you don't have enough data, you don't have the same population to deal with. The population that was there in 1991 in Srebrenica is not the same population that lived in Srebrenica in 1995. There's a series of documents that people moved out before 1995, that people moved in from neighbouring municipalities during the entire period from 1992 when this was a free zone. So this population, even if you had the exact figures - and also I came across some information among experts saying that it is considered to be 40.000. I'm not challenging that. But within these 40.000 there is a part only of the inhabitants that lived in Srebrenica in 1991 but then there are also those who came from Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Visegrad and so on and so forth. So it is not only -- it is no longer the same population. So to calculate anything in terms of age, et cetera, for Srebrenica and to assess how many inhabitants of Srebrenica there were in Srebrenica, then no one can do that. It can only be done at an aggregate level. This aggregate level is methodologically correct, and you can say there were this many in 1991, this many in 1995, went missing, died, et cetera, from the total population of 1991. And this is the total number of victims from different areas. It is that percentage. That's it. And this is how it is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page you have also a table number 10. Is there anything that you need to add to anything that you just talked about in relation to that table as to what it demonstrates?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regarding the population and since they're referring to a broader context, et cetera, et cetera, I thought it was intellectually honest to present it so that these victims, these people are not people who came from we don't know where, and from which entity. They are part of the entity of Eastern Bosnia and in order to show the ratio, how much this is in terms of Eastern Bosnia, I presented these shares, these percentages. And I said what this is like in terms of Srebrenica, what they considered to be Srebrenica, having separated only the male population from the total population figure. And, please, having taken into account the results provided by the OTP. In that case, these are the ratios obtained in relation to Eastern Bosnia, what it is like in -- compared to the total population, the male population, and what they considered to be Srebrenica when they say how many victims there are and when they make a list of victims. This is what it looks like in terms of the total population from 1991, and this is what it looks like in terms of the male population from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what impact on the vitality of the population would these figures have?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, with the most profound respect to each and every victim, from a demographical point of view these are not indicators that could significantly affect the vitality of the Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia, Bosnia in general, and these municipalities around Srebrenica. In my view, migrations have had a far more adverse effect. Migrations that took place after the war as well. Migrations have a significant effect. During all research, before the war as well, migrations took away a lot more young people, fertile people, who left and the persons who were left there were persons who were done with the reproduction cycle. To this day, I believe that migration -- as far as migrations are concerned, they have to this day, a far more adverse affect than these mortality effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last document to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question about this document. You gave the proportion, the percentage, with one number after the comma. Isn't it methodologically right that if it's more than 10.75 that you make it 10.8 and if it's less than 10.75, you make it 10.7. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my country, all information of this kind is provided with one decimal point. I don't think that another one would mean anything different. Now, is it 10.7 per cent or is it 10.70 per cent ... if you allow me, I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be 10.79, if you reduce to one digit after the comma would it be 10.7 or would it be 10.8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10.8 or 10.75. It can be checked. When I work and if I get 10.75, I round it off to 10.8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the other set of figures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is not 0.000 percentage of something that would affect something else. So this is how I work. This is how I have worked ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Yes, then have you an opportunity to correct the 10.79 into 10.8. Because that's the outcome, 10.79, if you divide the one by the other. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I do when I work on these percentages. You can check that. I automatically turn them into that. I do not give two digits after the decimal point. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop there. I did verify it. And it was 10.79. And you told us that you would automatically then make it 10.8, whereas, you made it 10.7. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall check. I do apologise if I did that. For the most part, I don't do it that way but I will check.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear part of your answer but I don't know how to go back to it to recreate it now, having gone beyond that. I note the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not insist and all the parties can make the division and see what the outcome is, and the witness apparently said that if she made a mistake that she apologises for it and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can call up 1D5350.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if it assists I do have a hard copy of this document for the witness, since we will be looking at a table later on. Looking at what we have on the screen, Professor, can you tell me what kind of publication this is?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official statistical publication of the statistical agency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at table number 2 which starts on page 3, and ... I note that the last part is cut off so if we could have page 4 on the right-hand side since the table has both English and B/C/S. If we can have page 4, that will be the continuation of this part that has been cut off on the right-hand side in the printing of the publication. And now looking at Table 2, could you explain for us what this data represented here tells us about -- about the populations in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information about vital events, the number of births and the number of deaths from which information about the natural movements of the population is derived. As you can see, it begins with 1996. There is no information about the years of war. And you can see that the natural population growth is positive until 2004. It decreases but it's positive all the time. And I stress that we are talking about the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina in total, not broken down by ethnicity. So this population growth was positive, which is good, because it means that natural renovation of the population continues. The war did not lead to a horrible decline and a negative birth rate. Negative birth-rate means that more people die than are born. And I wanted to show that in terms of vitality for Bosnia-Herzegovina - this is up to 2004 - there is no problem as long as the birth-rate remains positive. Drastically, it does decline from 1996 to 2004, but apart from deaths, there is also the effect of migrations, and in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, migrations have been very important as a factor in the decline of the population growth. And I see, coming back to the question of His Honour Judge Orie, that I, indeed, made a mistake with that decimal digit. I apologise for not using two decimal digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have used one, but you should have properly used it. That was the issue. Can I ask you one short question before we take a break. Does the vitality after the war tell us anything about the birth-rate during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only have birth-rates after the war here and I cannot claim what happened during the war. But if this is after the rate [as interpreted] -- these are relatively high birth rates. In Western European countries you have much lower birth rates and higher mortality rates. These are relatively satisfactory birth-rates compared to any developed Western European country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have not -- well, the reason why I was asking is that you said the war did not lead to horrible decline and a negative birth-rate. That -- you have demonstrated that for the period after the war, which I could imagine has got something to do with overcoming the war increases vitality, I do not know but that's something I could think of. But whether the vitality was affected during the war, therefore, could not be demonstrated by these figures. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the objective here was not to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. I just asked this question in relation to one of your answers. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Mr. Ivetic, I don't know where you are on the 15 but you really should complete --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One question. I just want to tender this document and one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps put that question now. Witness, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic has only one question so we decided not take the break but, first, to hear your answer to that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could first tender this document before we lose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5350 receives exhibit number D1213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Tabeau testified at this trial at transcript page 19.396, line 20 and onwards as follows. I will read it so you get the translation: "Q. So let's take them one by one. Do you believe that the use of the term 'massacre' in a demographic report is appropriate? "A. Yes. The word of 'massacre' is used in the second-last paragraph. It is used in the 2009 Srebrenica report. That is related to about 8.000 individuals who went missing during the fall of Srebrenica and subsequently a large number of them were exhumed from mass and other graves in the territory of Srebrenica and neighbouring municipalities. And subsequently a large number of them were identified through DNA analysis and, in this way, the circle closed. I think this is very good reason, in my eyes, to call Srebrenica and victims of the fall of Srebrenica a massacre." Now, I'd like to ask your professional opinion as a demographer, if Dr. Tabeau is acting within the scope of the field of demography in using this type of analysis for massacre.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Tabeau -- I don't know whether she knows this or not, and according to which definition she uses the word "massacre," but I'm sure that all the violent deaths, and their list of names contains only violent deaths, I suppose, divides into murders, suicides and accidents. Dr. Tabeau, looking at that list and picking a certain name, doesn't know whether that person was killed in combat, whether they committed suicide or was killed in an accident. She doesn't even know if any natural death is involved. So if she doesn't know anything about that and cannot get information, how can see say that it is a massacre? The person who died in combat or suicide or a person killed by stepping on a land-mine was certainly not massacred. I don't know what, in her book, is a "massacre," but I suppose that it has to be a mass execution. Dr. Tabeau does not even know how many people were executed, nor did the sources she had at her disposal and she used -- no, not the ones she had at her disposal because I don't know what she had. But she cannot even draw conclusions about people who were killed in executions, just like she cannot derive a conclusion as to how many people in total were killed in other ways, but there are some data in the demographics office, that there were accidents, that there were people killed in combat, that there were cases other than killings. I don't know how many such cases there were, but they certainly existed. And if they existed, then I don't understand Dr. Tabeau, when she explains that the whole circle is completed when a person was found in a mass grave, I cannot accept that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank You, Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not supposed to speak aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your indulgence. That's the end of my direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, we'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, when you'll be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud. We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll deal with a short preliminary matter. That is, about the replacement of P3468. On the 18th of August of this year, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to verify the English translation of P3468. On the 19th of August, the Prosecution advised the Chamber and the Defence, via an e-mail that a revised English translation had be replaced with doc ID 0425-8552-A-ET. On the same day the Defence responded stating that it did not object and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P3468 with the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for a clarification I've been told that the doc ID which begins with 0245 in the transcript should actually read 0425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's what I read, but I'm not certain about it. But I agree that it should be 0425-8552-A-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. File. You find him to your right. Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. File, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could please have D1210, we're going to start talk a little bit by your background and preparation for your testimony in this case. Are you able to read and write as well as speak and understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My English is poor, in terms of speaking or any other skill.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: On your CV which we're looking at now, it says that from 1992 to 1999, you were an expert associate in the institute of humanities centre of demographic research. Is that a Belgrade-based institution?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And then from 1999 to 2014, you were an associate professor at the university college of geography in Belgrade. I note that yesterday at T38133, you verbally updated this part of your CV to reflect your retirement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now the academic rank of associate professor in Serbia is denoted in Serbian as [B/C/S spoken]; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And there was also a lower academic rank in Serbia called docent or senior lecturer; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And isn't it true that contrary to what you've just told us and what's written on your CV, you only became associate professor in 2005; and before that, starting in 1999 you were a docent or senior lecturer?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I only don't know as opposed to what.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, the CV that you've presented to this Chamber and that you affirmed yesterday as complete and accurate, as well as your testimony today has overstated your qualifications for the period from 1999 to 2005; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. This is about work experience, and I have been at the university from 1999 to 2013 and I put in the latest title. It doesn't mean that I am an associate professor from 1999. It's the position where I have been employed, stating the latest title that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So it's your position that a biography or a CV should only include the most recent position that you've held at any given institution.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The question here was about work experience, where I have worked and where I worked earlier, and in which position. Senior lecturer and associate professor are teaching positions. They differ only inasmuch as you start in a teaching position as a senior lecturer, and then, after you meet certain qualifications, such as papers and other, you get the next level, or you have to be reelected, et cetera. Maybe I should have written 1999 to 2005 senior lecturer, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's move on. I think the facts are clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 33019, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, when this comes up, you will see that this is your CV from the last time that you testified before this Tribunal which was back in -- in November 2008 in the Prlic case. At the bottom of page 1, you see a category heading: Selection of published scientific works followed by a list of 17 documents that you authored or co-authored between 1990 and 2007.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you see at the bottom of the page, there's a heading that says: Selection of published --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now during your testimony in that case, you stated that the works you listed on this CV were the ones that had been published in journals. That was correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's customary to get a transcript reference if referring to a transcript from other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That would be from the Prlic case T34994, lines 21 to 23, from the 25th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in professional and scientific journals.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And then you were asked whether any of those works had been the subject of international peer review and your response was: "No, they were not subject of international peer review because all the journals that I listed are published in Serbia in journals that are significant, scientifically significant at national level, so they did not undergo international peer review but they were reviewed by relevant scholars in the area where I live." That was correct as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does the word "reviewed" mean that somebody wrote a review of my paper or viewed it on the Internet? If you mean the writing a review, reviews of my work were written by our national experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're talking about international peer review before publication takes place. The process of selecting a publication. That was the context of the questions in the Prlic case.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a paper is published in our journals, they are reviewed by our national experts. My paper was reviewed by national experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to cut matters short, was that after publication or before publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before. Not a single paper can be published anywhere before receiving a review required for publishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now if we can return to your current CV for this case, D1210, you'll see if we go to page 2 in both versions, you'll see that your publications have disappeared and have been replaced with a the statement under the heading: Research work that says you published over 70 scientific and expert works and studies in demography, ethnography and population statistics. So my first question is: Is your answer from the Prlic case still correct today in other words is it still true that you have not published any articles in scientific journals that were the subject of international peer review before publication?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I just didn't write this again. In the meantime, I published in a journal of the Russian Academy of Science. I suppose you would treat that as international.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And what's the citation for that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. It's the citation for what? Why didn't I state it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could you provide the title and the date and the exact journal name.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. But I cannot do it off the cuff. I don't want to make a small mistake and then appear as not speaking the truth. I can provide the exact name of the journal to the Court later. I can leave it with the Defence counsel and he will pass is on to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're supposed not to further have contact with Defence counsel. So there are two options. The one is that you write it down and give it to the Victims and Witness Section which I think would be preferable and the Victims and Witness Section would then give to the parties and to the Bench so that Mr. File has an opportunity to check. So could do you that preferably as soon as possible this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am unable to do that in afternoon. I don't have the journal with me so as to be able to exactly reference the title of the journal and of the article and of the year. I can do that at some later point. I can also forward the details of a book I have published in the meantime. I don't know what the view of the OTP would be on that. It was commissioned by the European Union and the Serbian ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. Give whatever additional information you have. But I urge you to do it this afternoon because the communications these days are such, I take it that through the Internet or in any other way it must not be that difficult to find the publication and where it was published and when it was published. I often forget about my own publications but I usually find them rather quickly again. So you are invited to do your utmost best to provide that information this afternoon. At the same time, of course, the parties could do as a search as well -- and if you find anything, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I live in a single household. I have no one to ask to pick up this or that book to give me the details. There's no one that can I ask that to do in my apartment. Perhaps I can speak to the faculty, since I retired in the meantime but I'm no longer on their list. That is the problem. The Internet is not a problem. I just don't know how I would be able to do it today over the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who contact to enter my apartment and locate the publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But most journals have published the content of their volumes on the Internet. That's at least what is my experience. So would you try to do your utmost best and whether it's the faculty or someone else --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that. It didn't occur to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'll ask the Victims and Witness Section to get in touch with you so as to -- to finalize that and you provide the information to them. Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Final question about your CV. You have a category titled: "Other professional activities" on this page that we're looking at where you describe being a member of various professional bodies and having been a witness here and in Sarajevo. And this list of professional bodies includes all of the professional organisations that you are a member of or have ever been a member of; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of which I was. I'm still a member of some.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And are all of those organisations based either in Serbia or the Republika Srpska in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are all either in the Republic of Serbia or in Republika Srpska, but the European Centre for Peace and Development is also located or, rather, it has a branch office in Belgrade. Its headquarters are not in Belgrade. Just part of the organisation is there. It functions under the auspices of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Just a few broader preliminary questions. As a university - we're done with this document, by the way - as a university associate professor in demography until 2014, do you try to stay informed about what colleagues at other universities around the world are researching and writing about, for example, by reading articles that are published in prominent international peer-reviewed journals in your field?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Both as the senior lecturer and the associate professor or when I was outside the teaching profession. All articles or papers that I hear of which are within my sphere of interest is something that I review. If they are in English, I asked for them to be translated, and I do read them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 38138, you said: "I provide footnotes for everything that I refer to." Now just to clarify that, do you agree that when writing a scientific article or expert report for a court case, it is important to give citations that support claims that are made in the article or report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote. I do not provide footnotes without a direct quote. I agree that other people need to be quoted and referenced in the footnotes. I never drew my own conclusions about somebody else's words. I specifically quote the part I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Does that mean that if you make a claim in an article or an expert report that you write and it's not directly quoting a specific source that you might not put a footnote with a citation to that source?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that it has never happened, but I do my utmost for it not to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, I need three minutes in private session. Therefore, I'd like to invite you to stop a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Before we do, may I tender 65 ter 33019 which was the CV from 2008 that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection. But I note most of the documents on the list are not available to the Defence in e-court so we can please fix that so I can look at them, that would be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they not uploaded, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Everything should have been released. That's the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's apparently what Ms. Stewart confirms by nodding. I take it that the parties will resolve this matter before 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sooner than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind you that it would be highly appreciated, Ms. Radovanovic, if you provide the titles and any additional information and give it to the Victims and Witness Section. They will certainly also assist you in getting access to the Internet if you need that. Apart from that, I would like to instruct you as I did yesterday you should not speak or communicate in whatever way apart from for the purposes we just discussed, with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Madam Registrar, could you please assign an exhibit number to the 2008 CV which was 65 ter 33019.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit number P7512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7512 is admitted into evidence. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 26th of August, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of August, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
